Interviewer:	I’ll tell you a little bit more about what we’re actually doing. We’re basically interviewing women across all the different engineering subjects and mainly people who are going on placement but we’re also interviewing people who aren’t going on placement to find out why they’re not going on placement. But the reason we want to interview people going on placement, is to look at women’s first experience of the engineering industry and we’re looking at what impact that has on their career intentions. So the ultimate aim is, at the end of it, we’ll get some ideas about what women actually expect and what the reality is. And we’re going to write a practical guidance document on how to make things better.

Subject:	Oh wow, cool.

Interviewer:	For the Engineering Council and engineering companies and we’re going to involve them towards the end of the project, in the actual research. OK I’ll start asking you a few background questions about why you wanted to go into engineering and that quite of thing. You’re doing a civil engineering course aren’t you?

Subject:	Uh huh…

Interviewer:	And what ‘A’ levels did you do?

Subject:	I did maths, physics and PE and ‘AS’ history …

Interviewer:	OK, what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Erm, it was just a big normal comprehensive school.

Interviewer:	Not an all girls’ school then or anything like that?

Subject:	No

Interviewer:	Ok, have you got any previous work experience?

Subject:	Yes – what in engineering?

Interviewer:	Either.

Subject:	Erm, well I was a waitress for 4 years, and then I was sponsored by a company and I went on a summer placement and worked in a sewage works. So I’ve had (?) experience really, of engineering and things like that, which is interesting and I’m going – yeah I’m doing the year out with the same company and I’m – I get money from them, each term, well each semester, and at the end I think I’m contracted to work for them, if they want me to, for like a couple of years. So I just signed up for it – it’s all experience, at the end of the day, isn’t it.

Interviewer:	What do your parents do are either of them engineers at all?

Subject:	No, my dad’s a nurse, my mum’s a social worker.

Interviewer:	OK so why did you decide to do engineering?

Subject:	It was quite interesting actually. I was doing my ‘A’ levels, I was like – I did my ‘A’ levels – I started doing Physics, which was totally – because I had a bet with my mum (laughter) I bet I don’t get A’s in sciences, she said if you do, I think you should do physics. I said OK, I bet you, I don’t, so I’ll do physics if I get A’s. So – I wanted to do Psychology, but er – I went to see a careers advisor and she said, have you thought of engineering? And I was like, I don’t even know what that is and she says well, it’s like when people make things that you know – they – that people use and things like that. And I said, that sounds really interesting and then I went on a – do you know Head Start? – I don’t suppose you’ve heard of Head Start, it’s like an engineering kind of - seventeen year olds getting experience kind of thing.

Interviewer:	 (I’ve heard of?) different things that are on the same lines, yeah.

Subject:	Well, I kind of – I don’t know how I got into it, but I signed up for that so in the middle of like 2 years, I went on a week long finding out about engineering thing in Colorado. Erm, and that was really good, so you chose 2 – you wanted to look at and then you did a 3rd day and looked around all the other ones (yes). So the first day, I looked at civil, which is the one I kind of knew a bit about. Second day I looked at mechanical and the third day I looked at physics – doing actual physics – aero and electrical and I came out with liking civil the best really. Erm, I liked the management aspect best, so I just applied and that’s why really. And I couldn’t really think of anything else I wanted to do. I always wanted to be a PE teacher but you know, there’s not a lot to do with PE, is there really (laughter) And here I am. (OK). It was quite general as well, so I thought well – you know, and I’ve heard you can get jobs in other fields as well if you do engineering, so …

Interviewer:	So the biggest influence were the careers people, would you say?

Subject:	Probably. Also, in my physics class, everyone else was doing an engineering course. They wanted to do at Uni – so they were quite a big influence as well, and my Physics teacher as well – she’s a civil engineer. Erm, careers advisors kind of put the idea in my head and I had a – like went on research on my own and stuff. My parents said they didn’t have a clue.

Interviewer:	But they supported your decision?

Subject:	They were like, oh that’s interesting – and I’m like, they did a lot, they just looked at league tables and things and heard it was really good and my granddad, who was an engineer or something so yeah – they kind of thought it was a really good idea. They did Open University, so they thought you know, do a degree now.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think it is that actually appeals to you about the engineering then?

Subject:	Hmm, I don’t know. I mean I – I would be lying if I said I hadn’t thought, I’m a girl and therefore I’ll get a job – because I have. That’s like – you know, that’s kind of like up there. I don’t know – I kind of like the engineering – the way it’s so general and you know you can go into consulting or you can go into like contracting, you can go on site, you can work in a design office, you can work even higher than that. It’s just so general – there’s so many aspects to building – I mean (lost words). I mean like you’ve got so many fields – you’ve got trains, roads, dams, bridges, you know. There’s so much stuff you can do – and that’s – that appealed to me a lot. My mate’s doing aero and all she does is aeroplanes. I mean it’s what she loves but it seems a bit narrow.

Interviewer:	I’ve spoken to quite a few people doing mechanical and they’ve said they’re interested in going down the aero route but were advised against doing that degree because it’s so specific.

Subject:	It’s so specific and now – now there’s all the problems going, well there’s not much – I mean there’s work for them but not as much as there was. Kind of. So there’s other problems about.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anything that you particularly didn’t like about, say mechanical engineering, that…?

Subject:	I didn’t understand it really. I didn’t understand like how engines work. I’ve never – my dad’s not very engineering minded – he’s never really taught me, like about engines and stuff. So I just think I didn’t understand it, because we did a Go – Kart. They showed us how to make a Go-Kart and I just didn’t get it at all, whereas things like building you can understand that it goes foundations, you know, brick this as well – these certain things. Yeah, so I’m just not good for things like mechanical.

Interviewer:	Ok, how did you decide to come to [this university]?

Subject:	Erm, I was initially interested in sports aspect of it to be honest, doing PE and things like that. My mum’s like no way, you’re not doing that. She thought that doing PE was too narrow and there’s like so many people doing PE isn’t there? So I – well I applied to [this university], thinking oh I would never get in or if I did – well, I got 6 offers you see and I knew I would, so I knew I could have the pick of them. It’s pretty up myself, isn’t it? - like knowing I’d get them. But I applied to [university 1], [university 2], [university 3], [this university], [university 4] and [university 5] and went to all of them. And erm [this university], over like the time I applied, it just – it appealed to me more and more, I think. Especially when I came to see it. I really liked the campus – the way it was. And then my mum was like you know, civil engineering is really good at [this university]. And I was like, oh OK, I didn’t really know that. And that’s why really.

Interviewer:	Yeah, were you interested in the fact that you could do a placement year at [this university] – because I went to [university 5] and I’ve got friends that did civil engineering and for instance there they don’t do work placements?

Subject:	Really, I didn’t know that. I mean I was – when I came up on Open Day they did say we do do sponsorship. And that appealed to me as well, for the M. eng erm, so that appealed to me and also, I didn’t do a year out on purpose because I knew I’d be doing one. I didn’t know [university 5] didn’t do one.

Interviewer:	I don’t think (lost words) It’s quite interesting that for some universities [the placement] is a really big thing, like here – there’s quite a wide variety of subjects that you can do here.

Subject:	You can do everything – you can do politics and stuff as well. Yeah, it’s really good.

Interviewer:	OK, did you realise that, when you first applied to do engineering, that it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	And did it bother you?

Subject:	No. I did PE, maths and physics for my ‘A’ levels

Interviewer:	Did it ever bother you when you were doing A levels that they were…?

Subject:	Not – I got used to it, you know, and it didn’t bother me at all because I get on with guys really well anyway. And er, it’s kind of like – you kind of have a good thing really because they try and get more girls in, so usually that’s OK and I think that’s pretty well the reason I got in really. Erm, no it doesn’t bother me, but yeah I knew it would be. I knew there would be like 6 girls on the course.

Interviewer:	Do you think that perhaps more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

Subject:	It’s funny actually – I was thinking about that because er it seems that years go by and the same number of girls are doing it and I’m thinking why don’t they go into schools speak to the 16 year olds and 17 years that are doing like mathematical subjects (yes) because they don’t even know what it is.

Interviewer:	That seems to be what a lot of people are saying.

Subject:	I heard you can do like an engineering ‘A’ level and I didn’t know that.

Interviewer:	Really?

Subject:	Yeah, I just think while it can be done why not speak to everyone – not just the girls but the boys as well, ‘cos there’s not enough people doing it anyway. I think they said in like 10 years time or something there’ll be like no-one doing it because all the guys will have retired, or something.

Interviewer:	So what do you think could be done about increasing the numbers? Do you think it is through education?

Subject:	I do get these emails from this woman in mechanical engineering about women in engineering and like you can go to school and things but I never have time, it’s always funny times of the year. I think, as you get – it’s like young engineering students like – not like – maybe, people who’ve actually done their degree, go into schools and I don’t know when they do it though. If I think, they couldn’t do it in a lesson. That’s the problem with that – you couldn’t do it in assembly either. 

Interviewer:	I think that some companies have started doing that. I don’t think it’s to attract women particularly but I’ve spoken to someone who works at [company] and they’re involved in going into schools so that they can do stuff with the kids that lets them know what engineering is …

Subject:	That’s really good. They should do that everywhere I think, because I’m from the south, so we just did –everyone went in the navy or the army basically. (lost words) cannon fodder.

Interviewer:	What characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Extremely practical, I’d say – because we’ve just had the hardest semester and I’ve got so many stupid – well, there probably are reasons for doing maths, but we’ve got this module called hydraulics and I think one person out of the whole class is going to go into this field and it just seems so – some of the modules are just so specific. I just wish we had more practical modules like actually like – that involve what we’re going to be doing because most people are going to be Site Managers or like Construction Engineers and things like that and I just wish it was more practical, but on the degree you get the theoretical side.

Interviewer:	What kind of things…?

Subject:	More hands on – yeah, the kind of people that – it’s just – get a problem and just find it easier to think of – to use this approach. It’s just – you know.

Interviewer:	Do you think that would actually help you when you went into the work placement?

Subject:	Yeah, cos like – I know what it was like last summer. It was just – I mean they said, what do you get out of ergonomics structures and maths and like fluid mechanics and things. So I was like well, that’s not going to be any use to me is it, you know, like when you’re pouring loads of concrete in a hole. Like it’s just – I don’t know. I know you have to do it because it says in the ICE but it’s just annoys me.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think there’s any characteristics that are particularly male or female or…?

Subject:	I think guys are better at – it’s true they are good at spatial awareness, they can visualise distances but apart from that – I think girls aren’t given a chance, when they’re like younger. Like when they’re like in their teens and stuff and guys seem to be doing boy jobs, and girls do girls jobs and we come to [this university] and we’re all in the same labs and it’s just they’ve had a lot more experience working with metal or with like engines or things like that. It’s just – I think it’s just something – the experience of you growing up and things you get to – get to be doing. But when you get here, no, I think everyone’s equal really, apart from the experiences you’ve had, but no, I wouldn’t say anything like that. I’d say, guys I know, in the first place, they can’t think practical – they can’t think about, you know, what order like things go in – so experience, it’s just you need so much experience. Going away in the summer really helped me this year, even though it was the sewage works. You know, with what we’re doing.

Interviewer:	You’ve touched a bit on this already but do you think there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Yeah. Like you can (butter?) people up and stuff. Erm, I don’t think the lecturers particularly, you know, - either way. They don’t really see you as girls, they see you as an engineers. But employers like it, I think, because if you’ve got women engineers, it looks good for them, doesn’t it? Apart from getting jobs, I can’t see any other advantages really.

Interviewer:	OK, what about disadvantages?

Subject:	Erm, well I went on site, I’d never really experienced like any sexism here but I did on site and erm guys – ‘cos they’re older they don’t seem to have realised that there’s thing called political correctness and you know, it’s come up since they’ve been engineering. I just made tea the whole time, and I was expected to make tea and the guys – they were really nice to me, and I’ll tell you something really bad actually, telling you things like this but my – the guy who I was working with was called [name], and he – he bought me – he got me a really massive high vis jacket and I said to him about like 2 months in – I said why did you get me a really big one? He goes because most female engineers are fat and ugly and I was like, I can’t believe you’ve just said that. And I think – I felt like reportng him, because he was just so – things like that all the time. And I thought, well, if I’m working for this company and he’s in this area, I’m probably gonna be working for him again and I just don’t want any – you know – stigma attached to – I don’t want people to hate me. It’s not about (??) trouble making or anything but no, I mean….

Interviewer:	How did you feel about that at the time then?

Subject:	Oh I was just like (quite shocked?) I was quite shocked but I kind of laughed it off. You don’t want to make waves and stuff and I’m only like – I’m 19. I’m 19 – the youngest girl – the youngest person and only girl on site. You know – it’s something you’ve got to put up with I suppose. I suppose after a time you get used to it.

Interviewer:	Do you think you should have to put up with it though?

Subject:	No. But as long as I speak to him – I live – well, I don’t live on it, but I was on that site, [name] was my immediate boss, I couldn’t ring people up and say look it’s – oh, it’s really hard to explain because we’re like in a site that was 2 hours away from head office, so I didn’t really have any contact with anyone. I don’t even know them. So it was really hard.

Interviewer:	What about other people on the site, how did they treat you?

Subject:	Erm, kind of like flirting a bit really. They were quite flirty with me, which I put up with – I – it was all a bit – they didn’t mean anything by it, it was kind of like just a bit of fun really. It was alright – we kind of got – we became friends after a while. The labourers were the best, it was the managers that were like horrible. Well not horrible but …

Interviewer:	Is that what you expected that they’d be….

Subject:	I did expect – I thought the labourers would be more like rrrrrrrrrrrrrrrr, but they did it in jokey ways and I got to know after a while and we became friends – going out for drinks and stuff, but the managers – actually most of the managers were alright, it was just [name] that had a problem. I think he was just a dickhead really. He just seemed to be like that with everyone, so – you know.

Interviewer:	It didn’t put you off?

Subject:	Oh no, because he’s just one guy. Everyone else on there was absolute lovely, you know. They made a – I don’t know if they treated me differently because I was a girl – because I wouldn’t have known how he would treat a guy. I mean if I was a 19 year old guy on site, I still wouldn’t have any experience would I? I wouldn’t know anything so I’m sure he would have…you know. I know he was a bit patronising but then again I didn’t know anything so he probably should have been really.

Interviewer:	In terms of the course then, is it been what you expected?

Subject:	Mm, it is. It’s a bit less – it’s a bit more like maths and things like that – I wouldn’t say too much of it. I did expect it to be a bit more like group work – let’s design this. Whereas I’ve only had like about 3 modules of that and I’m in my 2nd year – at the end now. I mean the thing is – we didn’t have that much group work and although I don’t really like it, I know we have to do it, and I expected more of that in it. But, it’s OK.

Interviewer:	When you do have to do group work do you choose who you want to work with or do you get put into groups?

Subject:	Er, it depends. Sometimes – last year, we were put into alphabetical order. It’s – I don’t mind but there’s just – there was like one guy who appalled us, which was a bit awkward. And er – don’t quote that either. And er, no, I think being put in them’s OK, it’s just the fact that when you’re in alphabetical order you’ve got the sort of same people. It’s time – sort of like 3 times I was with this guy. If he was put into our lab group again – but we’re alright, we’ve got over it now. And er, but we’re also put into – we can also put ourselves into groups, which can be difficult, because I have a lot of – well a lot of my mates are on the course, and you know you’re with your mates and you’re doing group work. And it just gets – it can get a bit like if you get pissed off about the work – it’s not being you as a friend – its you as a work – I mean a work person. It’s Ok.

Interviewer:	OK, do you prefer to work with men or women or doesn’t it matter?

Subject:	It doesn’t matter at all. I mean I think guys – I don’t know why but they just seem to automatically think if you’re a girl, you’re bossy. You can do the bossing around. But no, I don’t mind. It’s like – as I say, I’ve known them for 2 years now and I get on with everyone like – you know – fine. So, I don’t really mind

Interviewer:	OK, have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Mmmm, I find I like things done a certain way and I end up doing it all – I don’t do it all myself but I like it – you know. I don’t know it’s hard because you’re sometimes – ah, I dunno really. No, not really. Oh, OK. It’s all OK, I think. You have to spend a lot of time together – you know, you just get a bit pissed off with each other sometimes, but no, it’s alright.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think has been the best and worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Best things – well I think the worst things is definitely the class exams, because they were so hard, and I worked really hard for them and I only got 54% and I was like – I’m not really happy about it because I’m on the MEng only if you get 60. Erm, that’s just – it’s just difficult when people erm, when you work really hard for things and you get the same as you would have done – if you know what I mean – when you’ve got guys who get like 70’s and they’re all like, oh I wish I’d done better. And you’re like – cabin packed? And – but, as I said before, I think the people that are more practical are probably the people who don’t do so well in these exams. They are so theoretical – well that’s a bad thing isn’t it? Yeah, good thing. I do go off the subject – I’m rambling.

Interviewer:	Do you think that your exam results are any reflection on the way that you’re taught?

Subject:	Er, yeah. I do actually because we’re taught to learn the exam questions and just remember – it’s just so not what we’re gonna do in real life you know?

Interviewer:	And do you think it should be more about the work rather than …

Subject:	Yeah, what you do across the year rather than your 2 hour exam that you or how well you’ve remembered this surveying technique that you never use for 5 years and things like that.

Interviewer:	How much course work have you had to do?

Subject:	Not much actually. This semester we’ve only had like 20% for each module. So that’s 80% exams, so if you do crap in the exams, which a few people do, then it really buggers you up because I did OK on the coursework – I got like A’s and B’s and it’s just so – it’s just that I wish they’d been worth more, really. Which is a bit upsetting, but what you gonna do? The best thing is probably – I do enjoy the 100% course work like modules because we had one last year – it was really good. It was engineering design, it was group work but it was so good. It was just we had to design, this like building, and we did everything for it and the structure and all the – it was just really good, it was really fun – 100% all the way.

Interviewer:	Do you think that helps prepare you more for the workplace?

Subject:	I think so yeah because you’re put into groups with people you don’t like, some you don’t know, some people of different abilities, some people who don’t work at all, and that’s the way it’s gonna be all your life, you know.

Interviewer:	That’s the thing about group work isn’t it? People probably don’t like it you know, you’re like…

Subject:	Hmm, yeah, it’s not that I don’t like it, I just – sometimes when people don’t pull their weight it really annoys me. I – sometimes I think oh peer assessments, but if you’re with your mates, you don’t want to give them less than 10. And it’s only worth like 1% any way, so I just give them all 10. (laughter)

Interviewer:	OK, have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	Er, yeah, one – [name] – she’s wicked.

Interviewer:	Is she? Does she treat you differently to the male lecturers?

Subject:	No, not at all.

Interviewer:	Any different style of teaching?

Subject:	Er, yeah, she’s more organised but that’s just women all round really, isn’t it? I don’t think she teaches – she’s quite a good teacher, though. I don’t think she teaches any differently – no, not really.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the male lecturers treat the male and female students the same?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	Male

Interviewer:	Would you rather have a female?

Subject:	No, - just not him. He’s terrible.

Interviewer:	Is he not approachable or…?

Subject:	Well, I’ve spoken to him twice and that was both in the first year. (lost words) and he’s just not a very good people person really. I just think he’s not very good with anyone but I’d rather. I don’t even think I’d rather have a female, I’d just rather have someone else I can probably talk to, so…

Interviewer:	Is there anyone else that you can go to talk to?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah [placement coordinator] yeah, he’s really cool to talk to. Such a help more than – like cos he teaches us construction design and he’s such a help and you just go and approach him and he’s really cool, about anything as well, anything to do with the course – not just the work. Yeah, he’s really good yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, who or what do you think has been the biggest influence on you since you started your degree?

Subject:	How do you mean? On my work or...

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	My friends probably. The guys on my course. If they say – if I say I think I’m not going to a tutorial, they go well I think I’m gonna go and I go, oh well I think I’ll go as well then. You know what I mean? But – it’s quite competitive on the course. You know, people know where people are in levels to themselves. So you don’t want to fall behind – you know what I mean? So yeah, definitely my mates on the course.

Interviewer:	Do you think it is competitive because it is so male dominated?

Subject:	No. I think it’s because it’s an engineers course. I mean – well, actually saying that, Nadia on aero, she says it’s really competitive and no one tells anything – no-one gives anyone help. It’s hard because my friend, my best mate is [name] and she’s a girl, and we tell each other everything about it, so…I’d say maybe a bit more competitive actually – maybe, ‘cos they’re all guys, because I’m not that bothered about where I am you know, but I’m just bothered like the fact that I got 54 and not 60. But maybe it is, I don’t know.

Interviewer:	OK, what aspects of university teaching and advice do you think will help you on your placement?

Subject:	Hmm, probably construction management – the module, ‘cos that’s kind of – that’s practical and about actually management and the way they do the project things – probably that. A couple of modules really help out but not as much…

Interviewer:	So it’s more the hands on…?

Subject:	More the actual, this is what’s going to happen on site, this is how we’re going to do our documentation modules instead of like maths.

Interviewer:	Do you think your summer placement will help you when you go on your work for your placement?

Subject:	Yeah, because a lot of things are cool, and I know what the programme is and things like that, because I wouldn’t have known that otherwise. But yeah, I definitely will – plus I know people and stuff.

Interviewer:	Yeah, will you be going back to the same site or…?

Subject:	No, that’s finished this summer – this Easter. I don’t know where I’m going actually. Hopefully it’ll be home somewhere.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel prepared and ready to go on the placement?

Subject:	Mm, well yeah, because it’s so different. I mean there’s no way to prepare every person for every project you’re gong to be on.

Interviewer:	Do you think that university could do anything or do you think that it is too diverse?

Subject:	Bit too diverse – way to diverse. I mean come back people have been working on trains and some people have been working in hospitals – there’s no way you can prepare for all of it. Also a lot of it’s like practical stuff, you know what I mean? There’s no way 2 years of – I guess – well in fact, I’ve learnt more in that summer than I did in the whole year of teaching and it’s just – I don’t think they can do it any other way really.

Interviewer:	OK, I think I know what the answer to this one is going to be but do you think that the educational experience reflects the reality of what it’s like in the industry?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it should have been organised so that it does more?

Subject:	Yeah. The thing is if the ICE say you’ve got to do this stuff you’ve got to do it because they’re the guys that (affiliating?) our course, but I don’t know. I think – because it’s like you’ve got 2 halves. You’ve got the contract – you’ve got contracting and you’ve got consulting and some people don’t go into design and need all the calculations we’re learning, but some people aren’t. But probably more aren’t…

Interviewer:	Do you have any optional modules or anything or is it all quite structured?

Subject:	Yeah, I think I’ve had one optional module.

Interviewer:	Is there probably a way of organising it better?

Subject:	I don’t know because I think in part D there’s a lot of optional modules, but I don’t know about ours, we only have one.

Interviewer:	Why did you decide to take the sponsorship route?

Subject:	So I could have some money.

Interviewer:	Any other reasons?

Subject:	No, not really. So I could get my foot in the door when I leave, without having to do interviews and things.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any disadvantages?

Subject:	Well, I’m now tied down. That’s the big problem. And also they got – they got off – they interviewed us after our first exams when we were – we’d just been at uni 4 months and they kept asking me questions like do you want to go for a job in contracting – I don’t know what on earth that means, you know? turns.text: You’ve touched a bit on this already but do you think there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.text: Yeah. Like you can (butter?) people up and stuff. Erm, I don’t think the lecturers particularly, you know, - either way. They don’t really see you as girls, they see you as an engineers. But employers like it, I think, because if you’ve got women engineers, it looks good for them, doesn’t it? Apart from getting jobs, I can’t see any other advantages really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what about disadvantages?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well I went on site, I’d never really experienced like any sexism here but I did on site and erm guys – ‘cos they’re older they don’t seem to have realised that there’s thing called political correctness and you know, it’s come up since they’ve been engineering. I just made tea the whole time, and I was expected to make tea and the guys – they were really nice to me, and I’ll tell you something really bad actually, telling you things like this but my – the guy who I was working with was called [name], and he – he bought me – he got me a really massive high vis jacket and I said to him about like 2 months in – I said why did you get me a really big one? He goes because most female engineers are fat and ugly and I was like, I can’t believe you’ve just said that. And I think – I felt like reportng him, because he was just so – things like that all the time. And I thought, well, if I’m working for this company and he’s in this area, I’m probably gonna be working for him again and I just don’t want any – you know – stigma attached to – I don’t want people to hate me. It’s not about (??) trouble making or anything but no, I mean….

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you feel about that at the time then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh I was just like (quite shocked?) I was quite shocked but I kind of laughed it off. You don’t want to make waves and stuff and I’m only like – I’m 19. I’m 19 – the youngest girl – the youngest person and only girl on site. You know – it’s something you’ve got to put up with I suppose. I suppose after a time you get used to it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you should have to put up with it though?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. But as long as I speak to him – I live – well, I don’t live on it, but I was on that site, [name] was my immediate boss, I couldn’t ring people up and say look it’s – oh, it’s really hard to explain because we’re like in a site that was 2 hours away from head office, so I didn’t really have any contact with anyone. I don’t even know them. So it was really hard.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about other people on the site, how did they treat you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, kind of like flirting a bit really. They were quite flirty with me, which I put up with – I – it was all a bit – they didn’t mean anything by it, it was kind of like just a bit of fun really. It was alright – we kind of got – we became friends after a while. The labourers were the best, it was the managers that were like horrible. Well not horrible but …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that what you expected that they’d be….

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I did expect – I thought the labourers would be more like rrrrrrrrrrrrrrrr, but they did it in jokey ways and I got to know after a while and we became friends – going out for drinks and stuff, but the managers – actually most of the managers were alright, it was just [name] that had a problem. I think he was just a dickhead really. He just seemed to be like that with everyone, so – you know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It didn’t put you off?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh no, because he’s just one guy. Everyone else on there was absolute lovely, you know. They made a – I don’t know if they treated me differently because I was a girl – because I wouldn’t have known how he would treat a guy. I mean if I was a 19 year old guy on site, I still wouldn’t have any experience would I? I wouldn’t know anything so I’m sure he would have…you know. I know he was a bit patronising but then again I didn’t know anything so he probably should have been really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: In terms of the course then, is it been what you expected?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, it is. It’s a bit less – it’s a bit more like maths and things like that – I wouldn’t say too much of it. I did expect it to be a bit more like group work – let’s design this. Whereas I’ve only had like about 3 modules of that and I’m in my 2nd year – at the end now. I mean the thing is – we didn’t have that much group work and although I don’t really like it, I know we have to do it, and I expected more of that in it. But, it’s OK.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you do have to do group work do you choose who you want to work with or do you get put into groups?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, it depends. Sometimes – last year, we were put into alphabetical order. It’s – I don’t mind but there’s just – there was like one guy who appalled us, which was a bit awkward. And er – don’t quote that either. And er, no, I think being put in them’s OK, it’s just the fact that when you’re in alphabetical order you’ve got the sort of same people. It’s time – sort of like 3 times I was with this guy. If he was put into our lab group again – but we’re alright, we’ve got over it now. And er, but we’re also put into – we can also put ourselves into groups, which can be difficult, because I have a lot of – well a lot of my mates are on the course, and you know you’re with your mates and you’re doing group work. And it just gets – it can get a bit like if you get pissed off about the work – it’s not being you as a friend – its you as a work – I mean a work person. It’s Ok.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you prefer to work with men or women or doesn’t it matter?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It doesn’t matter at all. I mean I think guys – I don’t know why but they just seem to automatically think if you’re a girl, you’re bossy. You can do the bossing around. But no, I don’t mind. It’s like – as I say, I’ve known them for 2 years now and I get on with everyone like – you know – fine. So, I don’t really mind

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mmmm, I find I like things done a certain way and I end up doing it all – I don’t do it all myself but I like it – you know. I don’t know it’s hard because you’re sometimes – ah, I dunno really. No, not really. Oh, OK. It’s all OK, I think. You have to spend a lot of time together – you know, you just get a bit pissed off with each other sometimes, but no, it’s alright.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think has been the best and worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Best things – well I think the worst things is definitely the class exams, because they were so hard, and I worked really hard for them and I only got 54% and I was like – I’m not really happy about it because I’m on the MEng only if you get 60. Erm, that’s just – it’s just difficult when people erm, when you work really hard for things and you get the same as you would have done – if you know what I mean – when you’ve got guys who get like 70’s and they’re all like, oh I wish I’d done better. And you’re like – cabin packed? And – but, as I said before, I think the people that are more practical are probably the people who don’t do so well in these exams. They are so theoretical – well that’s a bad thing isn’t it? Yeah, good thing. I do go off the subject – I’m rambling.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that your exam results are any reflection on the way that you’re taught?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah. I do actually because we’re taught to learn the exam questions and just remember – it’s just so not what we’re gonna do in real life you know?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And do you think it should be more about the work rather than …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, what you do across the year rather than your 2 hour exam that you or how well you’ve remembered this surveying technique that you never use for 5 years and things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How much course work have you had to do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not much actually. This semester we’ve only had like 20% for each module. So that’s 80% exams, so if you do crap in the exams, which a few people do, then it really buggers you up because I did OK on the coursework – I got like A’s and B’s and it’s just so – it’s just that I wish they’d been worth more, really. Which is a bit upsetting, but what you gonna do? The best thing is probably – I do enjoy the 100% course work like modules because we had one last year – it was really good. It was engineering design, it was group work but it was so good. It was just we had to design, this like building, and we did everything for it and the structure and all the – it was just really good, it was really fun – 100% all the way.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that helps prepare you more for the workplace?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so yeah because you’re put into groups with people you don’t like, some you don’t know, some people of different abilities, some people who don’t work at all, and that’s the way it’s gonna be all your life, you know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s the thing about group work isn’t it? People probably don’t like it you know, you’re like…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, yeah, it’s not that I don’t like it, I just – sometimes when people don’t pull their weight it really annoys me. I – sometimes I think oh peer assessments, but if you’re with your mates, you don’t want to give them less than 10. And it’s only worth like 1% any way, so I just give them all 10. (laughter)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you been taught by any female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah, one – [name] – she’s wicked.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is she? Does she treat you differently to the male lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Any different style of teaching?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah, she’s more organised but that’s just women all round really, isn’t it? I don’t think she teaches – she’s quite a good teacher, though. I don’t think she teaches any differently – no, not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the male lecturers treat the male and female students the same?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Male

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you rather have a female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, - just not him. He’s terrible.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is he not approachable or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, I’ve spoken to him twice and that was both in the first year. (lost words) and he’s just not a very good people person really. I just think he’s not very good with anyone but I’d rather. I don’t even think I’d rather have a female, I’d just rather have someone else I can probably talk to, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anyone else that you can go to talk to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah [placement coordinator] yeah, he’s really cool to talk to. Such a help more than – like cos he teaches us construction design and he’s such a help and you just go and approach him and he’s really cool, about anything as well, anything to do with the course – not just the work. Yeah, he’s really good yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, who or what do you think has been the biggest influence on you since you started your degree?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: How do you mean? On my work or...

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: My friends probably. The guys on my course. If they say – if I say I think I’m not going to a tutorial, they go well I think I’m gonna go and I go, oh well I think I’ll go as well then. You know what I mean? But – it’s quite competitive on the course. You know, people know where people are in levels to themselves. So you don’t want to fall behind – you know what I mean? So yeah, definitely my mates on the course.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it is competitive because it is so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. I think it’s because it’s an engineers course. I mean – well, actually saying that, Nadia on aero, she says it’s really competitive and no one tells anything – no-one gives anyone help. It’s hard because my friend, my best mate is [name] and she’s a girl, and we tell each other everything about it, so…I’d say maybe a bit more competitive actually – maybe, ‘cos they’re all guys, because I’m not that bothered about where I am you know, but I’m just bothered like the fact that I got 54 and not 60. But maybe it is, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what aspects of university teaching and advice do you think will help you on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, probably construction management – the module, ‘cos that’s kind of – that’s practical and about actually management and the way they do the project things – probably that. A couple of modules really help out but not as much…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So it’s more the hands on…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: More the actual, this is what’s going to happen on site, this is how we’re going to do our documentation modules instead of like maths.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think your summer placement will help you when you go on your work for your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, because a lot of things are cool, and I know what the programme is and things like that, because I wouldn’t have known that otherwise. But yeah, I definitely will – plus I know people and stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, will you be going back to the same site or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, that’s finished this summer – this Easter. I don’t know where I’m going actually. Hopefully it’ll be home somewhere.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you feel prepared and ready to go on the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, well yeah, because it’s so different. I mean there’s no way to prepare every person for every project you’re gong to be on.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that university could do anything or do you think that it is too diverse?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Bit too diverse – way to diverse. I mean come back people have been working on trains and some people have been working in hospitals – there’s no way you can prepare for all of it. Also a lot of it’s like practical stuff, you know what I mean? There’s no way 2 years of – I guess – well in fact, I’ve learnt more in that summer than I did in the whole year of teaching and it’s just – I don’t think they can do it any other way really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, I think I know what the answer to this one is going to be but do you think that the educational experience reflects the reality of what it’s like in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it should have been organised so that it does more?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. The thing is if the ICE say you’ve got to do this stuff you’ve got to do it because they’re the guys that (affiliating?) our course, but I don’t know. I think – because it’s like you’ve got 2 halves. You’ve got the contract – you’ve got contracting and you’ve got consulting and some people don’t go into design and need all the calculations we’re learning, but some people aren’t. But probably more aren’t…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have any optional modules or anything or is it all quite structured?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think I’ve had one optional module.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there probably a way of organising it better?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know because I think in part D there’s a lot of optional modules, but I don’t know about ours, we only have one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why did you decide to take the sponsorship route?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: So I could have some money.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Any other reasons?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really. So I could get my foot in the door when I leave, without having to do interviews and things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any disadvantages?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, I’m now tied down. That’s the big problem. And also they got – they got off – they interviewed us after our first exams when we were – we’d just been at uni 4 months and they kept asking me questions like do you want to go for a job in contracting – I don’t know what on earth that means, you know? So they kind of get you when you don’t really know if you’ve had enough information to think well, actually I don’t want to go (?) I want to go in that (?). Sometimes it doesn’t sponsor. So, I think they should have got us a bit later maybe, like after the first year but I’m not bothered now. It’s alright.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So how did you decide to go with that company? Did you apply to other companies?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I think I put down my top 4 or 5 and I got interviews with 3 of them, [company 1], [company 2] and [company 3]. And I got accepted by [company 1]. And I think I was accepted by [company 2] as well but because I put [company 2] lower than my first choice, I didn’t get accepted. So…I’m glad I got [company 1] really – everyone just got one I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What was it that attracted you to those companies then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it was the fact that they have got a big graduate training programme –you can get your chartered quite early. That’s what I thought – that’s what I thought we had to do and now I’m like you can do ok without being chartered – I’ve realised that now. But mm, I don’t know any other thing. I don’t know – ones I liked the look of the web site. They all seemed so similar to me, in the end, didn’t they, so I just ticked. And also I had a mate worked at [company 1] said they were quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you do much research into the company or was it just like …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It was just like web sites.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How involved were the university in the process?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They sorted it out. And we gave our application forms to [lecturer] and he sent off the – er to companies and they came back and interviewed us – so it was all sorted out by the university really, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, because you’re a sponsored student, do you have to go on a placement then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t actually think about that. I think you do. I think it’s kind of like, if you don’t then you’re really bad or something. I’m not sure.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So what sorts of things are you expecting to get out of the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well more idea about what I’m doing when I leave – like what field I want to go into – if any. Cos you can ask to be put into like 3 different places, depending on time of year – maybe that one, 3 months long (lost words) so I can get a bit more idea because I don’t want to end up in design if I like (?) on site. I’d like to be in an office as well. I also like some money really, so I can save up and not be so – in my last two years – so worried about things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think will be the worst things and the best things about being on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Bored.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Really?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ll be bored mentally – it’s like now I’ve got so much work on I don’t have time to think about anything. It’s really good – I love being busy. But I think the problem is it’s just all day – you come home in the evening and you’ve got nothing to think about, you know what I mean? Like doing your work – trying to keep learning stuff – like, that can be a problem for me. I get bored easily so…I try and keep myself occupied. I’m also tired – you get really tired. You feel really funny you know. But the good things will be learning more – just getting more practical experience really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it will improve your career prospects?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, it’s really good isn’t it? To say I’ve done one summer, another summer after, then a year in the middle of experience.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How would you say that the work does actually differ from being at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well it’s more adult world really, isn’t it? You don’t have your mates round you. You’re all living at home or probably will be. Hours – they forget, they come home at like – seven. Don’t go out as much either.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK, where do you see yourself in 5 years time then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh I don’t know, I really don’t know. I’m not one of these people that plan things. I’ll probably still be working for [company 1] but I – well I’m not sure if I want to be an engineer really. Sorry …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No that’s good – why?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Everyone’s so bored, the course is boring.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I didn’t mean it was good that you don’t want to be an engineer; I mean it’s just good that you’re telling me.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think, if you speak to a lot of girls they’ll say that they’re doing it – it’s a good degree – and they’re not sure they actually want to be it. What’s the question again?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I want to go travelling. Erm, but I’m not sure – I’m not sure what I’ll be doing really. I don’t know. Sorry.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’re not sure about that engineering bit yet then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m not too sure no, I’d like to try a bit more and see what – see how I go and see if I really like it. Cos I just think it’s really important to be in a job you really love because you’ve got like another 30/40 years of it and I just want to make sure I’ve got the right, you know, job.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that this placement here, will help?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I hope so. It should do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what would be your ideal career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Something where I could go to organise things, and it would involve a lot of travel.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you like to go and work abroad?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, love to – yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Any opportunities for that in the company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really because [company 1] have only got jobs in Egypt and Barbados and they don’t send graduates over there. And Iraq I think, which is a bit (dodgy?) but I might go over there later.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, they’re desperate for site managers everywhere. I’m not sure about anywhere else because I was working on site and the guys – there just – it’s just everyone seems so obsessed about how much money I can get and what car and pension and stuff. That’s all they cared about and I was like – if this is what you care about why are you – you know why the – oh, it just really bothers me. I mean if you work for money, then what’s the point? I mean you obviously work for money but I mean like….

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s more of a male thing than a female thing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It might be. I don’t know. I can’t really say because I’ve never worked in a female environment. I think it might be actually – a male thing. Hmm.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about once you have actually got into the industry, do you think the career prospects once you’re in a company are good?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so. Well I was like – good for moving around. It might be a problem though it you’re like – when you’re older older, say you’ve got kids and you’re married and stuff and there’s a lot of moving around. Like you go where the work is, don’t you?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So are these things that you’ve thought about?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well not really because I never plan to get married and have children but I think it obviously affects some girls.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, particularly because of the type of industry it is or long hours and things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, all the travelling and stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah I – cos we were saying like if you weren’t doing the course what would you be doing? And I was like, no idea. So that’s what we say when we’re starting to get bored.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you do anything differently?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I would – I wanted to be a psychologist but I’d have to choose psychology then and you know, I’m going right back then to when I was 16 and mum (?) Having a bet with your mum and things are different.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What 5 words would you use to describe the engineering culture or the characteristics of the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Pretty male dominated and it is – boys are very – this guy’s – well I know for a fact, guys are very immature together, you know what I mean. They seem to just revert back but that’s like – that’s like some (girls?) hang around with guys from the uni, not like 30 or 40 year old men. What 5 words let me think? I don’t know.
